title: The conquest of Mecca
hook: the Prophet ﷺ enters Mecca with ten thousand, almost without fighting, head bowed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khaybar and Safiyyah, a chief's daughter honored for her family. Your line was a mother of believers. Did you honor someone's background today? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

Years ago, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ slipped out of Mecca by night, hunted, with a price on his head. He looked back at the city and said he loved it, and would never have left if its people hadn't driven him out. Now it's Ramadan again. Mecca's allies have broken the peace of Hudaybiyyah, attacking a tribe allied to the Muslims. And one night the people of Mecca look out from the hills and see the valley below covered in campfires. The army behind them is ten thousand strong. The man they drove out has come back. Everyone in the city knows what conquerors do. Today: the conquest of Mecca.
screen: `YEARS AGO, BY NIGHT.` → `THE PEACE IS BROKEN.` → `TEN THOUSAND CAMPFIRES.`

segments.voice: That night, Abu Sufyan, Mecca's leader and the Prophet's old enemy, came out to see the camp, and before the army entered he had become Muslim. Sahih al-Bukhari says he was made to stand at a narrow pass and watch the army file by, tribe after tribe, until the Prophet's own company came past. And the Prophet sent him back to the city with an offer, recorded in Sahih Muslim: whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house is safe. Whoever shuts his own door is safe. Whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe. In other words: stay home, and nothing will happen to you. As the columns moved in, one commander, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, called out that today was the day of slaughter. Bukhari says the Prophet answered that Sa'd had it wrong: this is a day on which God will honor the Kaaba. The early biographers add that he took the banner from Sa'd, and they remember the reply as: today is the day of mercy. There was a brief clash on one side of the city. Otherwise, Mecca was entered almost without a fight. And the Prophet himself? The biographers describe him riding in on his camel with his head bowed so low, in humility before God, that his beard nearly touched the saddle. A companion in Sahih al-Bukhari remembered him reciting Surah al-Fath, the Victory, as he rode, softly, his voice wavering over the sounds. The surah that came after Hudaybiyyah, when it all looked like losing. He had left this city hunted, at night. He came back with its gates open, and he came back bowing.
screen: `ABU SUFYAN WATCHES THE ARMY PASS.` · `WHOEVER SHUTS HIS DOOR IS SAFE.` · `A DAY TO HONOR THE KAABA.` · `HEAD BOWED, RECITING AL-FATH.` · then, large: `HEAD BOWED ON THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enter a room humbly. Sit, and picture the next room you'll walk into where you have some standing: your team, your family, a class you teach, a place where people wait on your word. Picture yourself walking in the way the Prophet rode into Mecca: head a little lowered, voice soft, not taking up more space than you need. If you pray, you can remember that every win is God's. The bell holds the time.
The conquest of Mecca. The Prophet's return to the city that drove him out, with ten thousand, almost without fighting, and his head bowed. Today's word.
Your line: head bowed on the camel. Today, when you get something you wanted, receive it quietly, with your head a little lower. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the conquest of Mecca, in Ramadan, as the moment the Kaaba was cleared of idols and returned to the worship of one God, and it's often told as a lesson in humility and mercy in victory.

fork.setup: you've come back with ten thousand to the city that drove you out. one of your commanders shouts: today is the day of slaughter. what do you do?
options: take the banner and say: today is the day of mercy.
fork.reveal: Bukhari says he answered: this is a day on which God will honor the Kaaba. the biographers add: today is the day of mercy.

original.note: Arabic: the opening of Mecca. fath, the same word as al-Fath, the Victory.

trapdoor: what you thought: an army takes a city.
what it means: a return almost without fighting, safety for anyone who stayed home, and a leader riding in with his head bowed.
what a scholar hears: in Arabic it's the fath of Mecca, an opening; Muslim 1780 gives the safe-conduct, Bukhari 4280 the answer to Sa'd, 4281 the recitation of al-Fath.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1780 (whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house, shuts his door, or enters the mosque is safe)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4281 (reciting Surah al-Fath on his camel)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4280 (Abu Sufyan at the narrow pass; Sa'd's 'day of slaughter'; a day God will honor the Kaaba)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): head bowed; the banner; the day of mercy
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3925 (the Prophet's words of love for Mecca on leaving)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the teach told the 360 idols and 17:81 (day 279) and Bilal's adhan on the Kaaba (day 280); both moved out, and the teach now uses Bukhari 4280 (Abu Sufyan at the pass; the Prophet's answer to Sa'd) with a new head and match pair; cut the unsourced 'eight years' and 'enemy of twenty years'; the 'ten thousand' line no longer reads as ten thousand campfires; the 'day of mercy' reply attributed to the biographers in the fork too.
The commander who said 'the day of slaughter' was Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah; unnamed in the script. The 'day of mercy' reply is in the sirah (and partly in Bukhari 4280); confirm.
The brief clash (Khalid ibn al-Walid's column) is mentioned without detail; a few people were excluded from the amnesty, which the script doesn't mention. Keeper to decide whether to add.
'Eight years ago' counts from the Hijrah (1 AH to 8 AH); confirm.
Abu Sufyan's acceptance of Islam is usually placed the morning after he came to the camp; wording changed to 'by morning'. Confirm.
Day 279 is titled 'Idols from the House'; today already tells the 360 idols and 17:81. A Keeper may want to move that passage to day 279 to avoid telling it twice.
Tomorrow's forgiveness speech ('go, you are free') is deliberately not told today.
